title: A Bond to the Mutation Itself

scenes.tts: Ras was the standard example of an undruggable target. It holds its nucleotide with picomolar affinity. The cell keeps G T P near the millimolar range. So a competitor for that site must beat a very tight ligand, present in vast excess. And the known structures of Ras showed no groove deep enough to hold a small molecule.

scenes.tts: Kevan Shokat's laboratory went at the mutation itself. Glycine twelve has no side chain. One cancer mutation replaces it with cysteine. That puts a thiol on the surface of the protein: a reactive sulphur-hydrogen group.

scenes.visual: Ras with a plain Gly 12 spot; it becomes Cys 12 with an SH badge on the surface.

scenes.tts: The group held purified K Ras G twelve C in its G D P bound shape. It passed four hundred and eighty sulphur-seeking fragments over it, and weighed the protein to see what had attached. Two fragments attached to most of the protein. Normal K Ras, which has three cysteines elsewhere, showed no detectable reaction.
scenes.caption: The group held purified K-Ras G12C in its GDP-bound shape. It passed 480 sulphur-seeking fragments over it, and weighed the protein to see what had attached. scenes.tts: The crystal structure showed something new. The compound lay in a pocket beneath the switch two loop that no earlier Ras structure had shown. Once bonded, it tilts Ras toward holding G D P and gets in the way of Raf. The bond lasts for the life of that protein molecule, so the compound never has to out-compete G T P. In twenty nineteen, Canon and colleagues reported sotorasib, a drug for patients that bonds to the same cysteine. Keep this rule: bond to a residue only the mutant has.
